question: Three agents discuss quicksort average-case and worst-case behavior. Which position is best supported?
options: Quicksort uses no extra memory at all.
Pivot choice never affects quicksort performance.
Quicksort averages n log n but degrades quadratically in the worst case.
Quicksort always runs in n log n time.
gold_answer: Quicksort averages n log n but degrades quadratically in the worst case.
notes: Team-authored original item on quicksort average-case and worst-case behavior. Passages are team-authored derivations recorded under sciclaim-appx-A. Requires independent annotation and adjudication before any gate result is reported.

positions.answer: Pivot choice never affects quicksort performance.

claims.text: Already-sorted input with a first-element pivot causes quadratic behavior.

evidence.text: Degenerate pivots shrink the problem by one element per level, stacking n levels of linear work.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage stacks n levels of linear work, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Random pivots guarantee perfectly balanced partitions.

evidence.text: Random choice only balances partitions on average; unlucky picks still occur.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage allows unlucky picks, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: All O(n log n) sorts behave identically.

evidence.text: Constant factors and memory patterns were measured across the candidate sorts.

claims.verdict_rationale: Measuring differences cannot show identical behavior, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: Quicksort always runs in n log n time.

claims.text: Quicksort partitions around a pivot then recurses on both sides.

evidence.text: Each step places the pivot finally and sorts the smaller and larger elements independently.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage describes partition-then-recurse, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Quicksort is a stable sorting algorithm.

evidence.text: Partitioning swaps can reorder equal elements, so quicksort is not stable.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states equal elements can reorder, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Benchmarks on one input predict all inputs.

evidence.text: Timings were gathered over several input families.

claims.verdict_rationale: Gathering several families cannot show one input predicts all, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: Quicksort averages n log n but degrades quadratically in the worst case.

claims.text: Balanced partitions give n log n average performance.

evidence.text: Even splits at each level produce logarithmically many levels of linear partitioning work.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage counts logarithmic levels of linear work, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Recursion depth in quicksort is always logarithmic.

evidence.text: Degenerate partitions recurse n deep, which is why libraries bound the depth explicitly.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage gives n-deep counterexamples, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Sorting speed decides every system design.

evidence.text: Design trade-offs were weighed across the system review.

claims.verdict_rationale: Weighing trade-offs cannot show sorting decides everything, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.
